title: Why Barsac tastes the way it does

lede.text: Barsac makes one wine: a sweet white from grapes touched by noble rot. A particular microclimate lets the fungus behind it develop.

chapters.title: One commune in the Gironde
paras: Barsac is a single commune in the Gironde department. The grapes are picked there, and the wine is made and aged there.
By exception, nearby communes such as Sauternes and Preignac may also make and age the wine. The grapes still come from Barsac.

fly.label: The commune of Barsac
fly.caption: Grapes are picked, and wine is made and aged, within the commune of Barsac in the Gironde.

chapters.title: A microclimate for noble rot
paras: Particular microclimatic conditions allow the Botrytis cinerea fungus to develop. It gives the wines their typicity.
The supply of water favours the concentration of aromas in the berries. It gives the wines original nuances: fairly nervy, with persistent aromas of fruit.

chapters.title: Limestone underfoot
paras: Barsac stands apart because of the particular character of its soils. The limestone elements in the soil are linked to the mineral texture of the wines.

chapters.title: Picked by hand, pass by pass
paras: Barsac makes one kind of wine: a still white with residual sugar of at least 45 g/l, from botrytised grapes. In the mouth it is very rich and unctuous.
The grapes must reach a natural potential alcohol of at least 15%.
The main grapes are Semillon, Savagnin blanc, Sauvignon gris and Muscadelle.
Pruning is severe and set out for each grape, and must be done by 1 May. Vines are planted at a minimum of 6,500 per hectare.
Grapes are picked overripe, with noble rot, by hand in successive passes called tries. That gives a strong concentration of sugar in the berries. The maximum yield is 28 hl/ha.
